activity_context.topic_title: Integration by Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions

feedback.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $7{x}^{2}={(\sqrt{7}\,x)}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{7}\,x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{{(\sqrt{7}\,x)}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\sqrt{7}\,x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
